title: Screwy pirates
prompt: Five pirates just looted a chest of 100 gold coins and must divide the spoils. Being a surprisingly democratic crew, they agree on this rule: the most senior pirate proposes a distribution, then all five vote. If at least 50% approve (3 or more), the split stands. If not, the proposer walks the plank — and the next most senior pirate starts over.
Every pirate is perfectly rational: survival comes first, then greed, and — all else equal — fewer rivals on the ship is better.
The most senior pirate goes first. How many coins does he keep for himself?
hints: Start with just 2 pirates. The senior one always has 50% of the vote — himself. What does pirate 1 get?
With 3 pirates, the senior pirate knows pirate 1 gets nothing if his plan fails. How cheaply can he buy pirate 1's vote?
Work up to 4, then 5. In each case, the senior pirate only needs to bribe the pirates who would get nothing if he died.
solution_lede:
Game theory puzzles with recursive structure are almost always solved by starting from the simplest case and building up.

With 2 pirates, the senior pirate proposes 100/0 and wins 1-to-1 (50%). With 3, he knows pirate 1 would get nothing if the plan fails — so pirate 1 accepts any offer of 1 coin. Senior keeps 99.

With 4, the senior needs just 2 votes. He bribes pirate 2 (who gets nothing in the 3-pirate case) with 1 coin, keeps 99. With 5 pirates, the senior needs 3 votes total. He bribes pirates 1 and 3 — both get nothing under the 4-pirate arrangement — with 1 coin each. He keeps 98.

solution_steps.body: 2 pirates: senior proposes 100/0. Passes with his own vote (50%). Pirate 1 gets 0.
3 pirates: senior offers pirate 1 one coin — beats the zero he'd get if the plan fails. Keeps 99. Passes 2-to-1.
4 pirates: senior offers pirate 2 one coin (pirate 2 gets 0 in the 3-pirate case). Keeps 99. Passes 2-to-2.
5 pirates: senior offers pirates 1 and 3 one coin each (both get 0 in the 4-pirate case). Keeps 98. Passes 3-to-2.
